name: Quarter-sawn
process: The log is first quartered along its length, and boards are cut from each quarter so the growth rings stand steeply to the face (about 75-90 degrees; 45-75 degrees is rift-sawn). The face is then radial: a straight, close stripe of rings, and in oak the broad rays cut lengthwise as ray fleck. It is the wasteful cut: few boards, narrow boards, width bounded by the radius.

ringAngleToFace.source: WOODWEB Knowledge Base, 'Rays and Flecks in Oak' (forum digest of 30 September 2009; answer by Gene Wengert), https://woodweb.com/knowledge_base/Rays_and_Flecks_in_Oak.html
ringAngleToFace.note: Gene Wengert: quartersawn approximately 75 to 90 degrees; riftsawn 45 to 75

rayFleck.text: Quartersawn and riftsawn both show ray fleck, more pronounced on quartersawn; the only way to avoid fleck is to flatsaw.
rayFleck.source: WOODWEB Knowledge Base, 'Rays and Flecks in Oak' (forum digest of 30 September 2009; answer by Gene Wengert), https://woodweb.com/knowledge_base/Rays_and_Flecks_in_Oak.html

widthLimit.text: Narrower boards and considerable waste when a log is cut for quarter-sawn boards only.

text.text: Greater stability of form and size, with less cupping, less shrinkage across the width, less shake and splitting.

widthShrinkageOak.source: Meier, E. The Wood Database: English Oak (Quercus robur), https://www.wood-database.com/english-oak/ (read 2026-09-26)
widthShrinkageOak.conditions: a quarter-sawn face moves across its width by the radial shrinkage, green to oven-dry

ratioToPlainSawn.source: Meier, E. The Wood Database: English Oak (Quercus robur), https://www.wood-database.com/english-oak/ (read 2026-09-26)
ratioToPlainSawn.derivation: radial / tangential shrinkage = 4.7 % / 8.4 %: a quarter-sawn board moves across its width about half as much as a plain-sawn one

historicUse.text: Gustav Stickley championed quarter-sawn oak as structurally stronger, finer in grain and less liable to warp and check.

surface.figure: Parallel stripes of latewood; in oak, silvery flakes and ribbons of ray across the stripe, which read light or dark as the view turns.
surface.sheen: The ray flecks are cut cells lying in the face: they reflect differently from the fibre ground, so the fleck shimmers.

photograph: Straight, evenly spaced grain lines; ray flecks up to several centimetres long crossing them in oak.
Board widths modest and all similar.

unverified.reason: Fleck length and width follow the ray dimensions, which were not read in an oak anatomy source.
